message.p: How the correlated part of the uncertainty - an ISOCS .ecc file's baseline ("%err"), or the "Corr. %" column where one is shown - behaves from one energy to the next. It is a systematic modeling/geometry uncertainty, so an efficiency that is (say) 5% high at one energy tends to be high at nearby energies too - and how far that "nearby" reaches is what this sets.

ul.li: Fully correlated - it moves together across all energies (correlation ρ≈1). This is how GENIE treats the ISOCS uncertainties, and is the default.
Gaussian (log-energy) - the correlation falls off smoothly with the separation in ln(energy), controlled by the correlation length below.
Uncorrelated - each energy's correlated part is independent after all (ρ=0 between different energies).

message.p: It has no effect on the uncorrelated part - ISOCS Monte-Carlo convergence ("%cnvrg"), or the "Uncorr. %" column - which is independent between energies by definition.
The Gaussian correlation length, in natural-log-energy units, used when "Gaussian (log-energy)" correlation is selected. The correlation between two energies is ρ = exp(-½·((ln E₁ - ln E₂)/L)²).

For example, with L=0.35 two energies a factor of e (≈2.72) apart have correlation exp(-1/(2·0.35²))≈0.02, while energies 10% apart have correlation ≈0.96. Larger values make the uncertainty more correlated across energy.
